summary: This document extends signature-based authentication in the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2). IKEv2 had limited support for ECDSA, with only a few elliptic curve groups and a fixed hash algorithm tied to each. This standards-track update lets peers use a wider choice of signature and hash algorithms.

plainLanguage.summary: IKEv2 lets two routers prove their identity with a digital signature, and until now it had a separate authentication method for each kind of signature: one for RSA, one for DSA, and three for different kinds of elliptic curve. Each of those was tied to one fixed hash function, so every new curve or hash function would have needed a new method of its own. This RFC replaces all of that with one method that says, inside the signature itself, which algorithm and which hash were used, and adds a short message in which each end lists the hash functions it is willing to accept.

questions: what is ikev2 digital signature authentication
subtitle: One IKEv2 authentication method that carries the signature algorithm with the signature, so new hashes and curves need no new codes.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 has one authentication method for each signature algorithm: one for RSA, one for DSS with SHA-1, and three for different ECDSA curves, each tied to exactly one hash algorithm. Every new curve or hash function would need another method, and with ECDSA and DSS there is no way to extract the hash algorithm from the signature itself.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new authentication method, Digital Signature, whose authentication data is prefixed with an ASN.1 object naming the signature algorithm and the hash used. A Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS, sent in the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, tells the peer which hash algorithms the sender supports.
tldr.outcome: One method now covers RSA, DSA, ECDSA, RSASSA-PSS and anything that comes later, and the two ends may use different hash algorithms in different directions. The cost is that the curve and the hash can now be mixed freely, so the security of the result is that of its weakest part.

today: RFC 7427 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It adds the Digital Signature authentication method and the SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS notification to IKEv2, and it starts the IKEv2 hash algorithm registry.

sections.title: Why a New Authentication Method
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new IKEv2 authentication method to support signature methods in a more general way. The current signature-based authentication methods in IKEv2 are per algorithm: there is one for RSA digital signatures, one for DSS digital signatures using SHA-1, and three for different ECDSA curves, each tied to exactly one hash algorithm. This design is cumbersome when more signature algorithms, hash algorithms and elliptic curves need to be supported.

Three problems follow from that. In IKEv2, authentication using RSA digital signatures calls for padding based on RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, although the newer RSASSA-PSS padding method is now recommended. With ECDSA and the Digital Signature Standard, there is no way to extract the hash algorithm from the signature, so for each new hash function to be supported with ECDSA or DSA, new authentication methods would be needed; support for new hash functions is particularly needed for DSS, because the current restriction to SHA-1 limits its security, and there is no point in using long keys with SHA-1. And tying ECDSA authentication methods to particular elliptic curve groups requires an additional method for each new group, so the combination of new groups and hash functions would make the number of required methods unmanageable. The restriction of ECDSA authentication to a specific group is also inconsistent with the approach taken with DSS.

With the selection of SHA-3, it might be possible for a signature method to be used with either SHA-3 or SHA-2, which means that a new mechanism for negotiating the hash algorithm for a signature algorithm is needed.

The RFC therefore specifies two things. First, a new authentication method that includes enough information inside the Authentication payload data so that the signature hash algorithm can be extracted. Second, a method to indicate supported signature hash algorithms, which allows the peer to know which hash algorithms the other end supports and use one of them, provided one is allowed by policy. There is no requirement to negotiate one common hash algorithm, as different hash algorithms can be used in different directions if needed.

The new digital signature method is flexible enough to include all the current signature methods and to add new ones in future. To support that flexibility, the signature algorithm is specified in the same way that PKIX specifies the signature of a digital certificate, by placing a simple ASN.1 object before the actual signature data. This object contains an object identifier specifying the algorithm and any associated parameters. When an IKEv2 implementation supports a fixed set of signature methods with commonly used parameters, it is acceptable to treat the ASN.1 object as a binary blob that can be compared against the fixed set of known values; implementations can also parse the ASN.1 and extract the signature algorithm and its parameters.
sections.plainLanguage:
IKEv2 lets two peers prove who they are with a digital signature, and the signature is computed over a hash of the exchange, so the hash algorithm has to be known to both ends. The old design solved that with a separate authentication method for every combination: one for RSA, one for DSA, and three for particular elliptic curves.

That does not scale. Every new curve and hash function would need a method of its own, and with ECDSA and DSA there is no way to work out from the signature alone which hash was used. The DSA method is the worst affected, because it is pinned to SHA-1, so a long key buys nothing.

This RFC replaces the collection with one method. The signature names the algorithm and the hash used, and a separate message lists the hashes each end will accept.

sections.title: The Authentication Payload
sections.content:
The RFC specifies a new Digital Signature authentication method that can be used with any type of signature. Because authentication methods are not negotiated in IKEv2, the peer is only allowed to use this method if the Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS has been sent and received by each peer.

In this method, the Authentication Data field inside the Authentication payload does not just include the signature value, as in the other existing IKEv2 Authentication payloads. Instead, the signature value is prefixed with an ASN.1 object indicating the algorithm used to generate the signature. The object contains the algorithm identification OID, which identifies both the signature algorithm and the hash used when calculating the signature, and it can contain optional parameters that might be needed for algorithms such as RSASSA-PSS.

To make implementations easier, the ASN.1 object is prefixed by an 8-bit length field, so a simple implementation can know the length of the object without parsing it and use it as a binary blob compared against known signature algorithm objects. The ASN.1 used is the same as that in the AlgorithmIdentifier of PKIX, encoded using distinguished encoding rules. The algorithm OID inside specifies the signature algorithm and the hash function, both of which are needed for signature verification.

Currently only the RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm uses the optional parameters; for other signature algorithms the parameters are either NULL or missing. Some algorithms have two possible encodings, one with the optional parameters included but set to NULL and one where they are omitted. When encoding the ASN.1, implementations SHOULD use the preferred format called for by the algorithm specification: if the specification says preferredPresent then the parameters object needs to be present, although it will be NULL if no parameters are specified, and if it says preferredAbsent then the entire optional parameters object is missing.

The Authentication payload is the one defined in IKEv2: a Next Payload field, a critical bit with reserved space, a payload length, an Auth Method octet and reserved space, and the Authentication Data. The Auth Method octet specifies the method of authentication used, and Digital Signature has the value 14. It is computed as specified in Section 2.15 of RFC 7296 using a private key associated with the public key sent in the Certificate payload and using one of the hash algorithms sent by the other end in the Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS. If both ends send and receive those Notify payloads, and signature authentication is to be used, then the authentication method specified in this payload MUST be used.

The Authentication Data for this format holds three fields: an ASN.1 Length of one octet containing the length of the ASN.1-encoded AlgorithmIdentifier object, the Algorithm Identifier itself, which is of variable length, and the Signature Value, also of variable length. There is no padding between the ASN.1 object and the signature value, and for hash truncation the method specified in ANSI X9.62 MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage:
The Authentication payload is where a peer puts the proof of its identity. In the new method, that field holds two things instead of one: a short description of the algorithm used, and the signature itself.

The description is an object identifier, the same kind of label that a certificate carries to say how it was signed. Here it names both the signature algorithm and the hash function, because the receiver needs both to check the signature.

Before the description comes a single byte giving its length. That lets a simple implementation skip the description without parsing it and compare it against a list of values it knows, so an implementation need not understand the encoding at all if it only supports a fixed set of algorithms.

sections.title: Telling the Peer Which Hashes Are Supported
sections.content:
The supported hash algorithms that can be used for the signature algorithms are indicated with a Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS sent inside the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. This notification also implicitly indicates support of the new Digital Signature algorithm method, as well as the list of hash functions supported by the sending peer.

Both ends send their list of supported hash algorithms. When calculating the digital signature, a peer MUST pick one algorithm sent by the other peer. Different algorithms can be used in different directions. The algorithm OID indicating the selected hash algorithm, and the signature algorithm, used when calculating the signature is sent inside the Authentication Data field of the Authentication payload.

The Notify payload format is the one defined in Section 3.10 of RFC 7296. When a Notify payload of type SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS is sent, the Protocol ID field is set to 0, the SPI Size is set to 0, and the Notify Message Type is set to 16431. The Notification Data field contains the list of 16-bit hash algorithm identifiers from the Hash Algorithm Identifiers of the IANA IKEv2 Parameters registry, with no padding between them.
sections.plainLanguage:
The list of acceptable hash functions travels in a message that is sent in the first exchange of the connection, before anything is authenticated. Each end sends its own list, and the presence of the message also tells the peer that the new authentication method is understood.

There is no need for the two lists to match. When a peer signs, it picks one hash from the list the other end sent, and the one it picked is named inside the signature. The two directions of the connection may use different hashes.

sections.title: Choosing the Public Key Algorithm
sections.content:
The specification does not provide a way for the peers to indicate the public and private key pair types they have, which raises the question of how the responder selects a key pair type that the initiator supports. This information can be found by several methods.

One method is to indicate the key the initiator wants the responder to use in the IDr payload of the IKE_AUTH request sent by the initiator. In this case the initiator indicates that it wants the responder to use a particular key pair by sending an IDr payload that carries that information, and the responder has different identities configured, each associated with a key or key type.

Another method is a Certificate Request payload sent by the initiator. For example, the initiator could indicate in the Certificate Request payload that it trusts a certificate authority certificate signed by an ECDSA key, which implies that the initiator can process ECDSA signatures, so the responder can safely use ECDSA keys when authenticating.

A third method is for the responder to check the key type used by the initiator and use the same key type that the initiator used. This method does not work if the initiator is using shared secret or Extensible Authentication Protocol authentication, that is, if it is not using public keys. If the initiator is using public key authentication, this is the best way for the responder to ascertain the type of key the initiator supports.

If the initiator uses a public key type that the responder does not support, the responder replies with a Notify message with error type AUTHENTICATION_FAILED. If the initiator has multiple different keys, it may try a different key, and perhaps a different key type, until it finds one that the other end accepts. The initiator can also use the Certificate Request payload sent by the responder to help decide which public key should be tried. In normal cases, where the initiator has multiple public keys, out-of-band configuration is used to select a public key for each connection.
sections.plainLanguage:
The new method says which signature algorithm is in use, but it does not say which key the peer should use to sign. That question has to be answered separately, and the RFC lists three ways it can be settled.

The initiator can name the key it wants the responder to use, in the identity payload of its request. The initiator can say which kinds of certificate it trusts, and the responder infers from that which kind of key it may use. Or the responder can simply match whatever the initiator used, which works whenever the initiator used a public key at all.

If the responder cannot match, it refuses the authentication, and an initiator with several keys can try another one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tables 2 and 3 of the Recommendations for Key Management give recommendations for how to select suitable hash functions for the signature.

The new digital signature method does not tie the elliptic curve to a specific hash function, which is what the old IKEv2 ECDSA methods did. This means it is possible to mix different security levels, for example to use a 512-bit elliptic curve with SHA-1, so the security of the authentication method is the security of its weakest component, whether that is the signature algorithm, the hash algorithm or the curve. This complicates the security analysis of the system.

IKEv2 peers have a series of policy databases, described in Section 4.4 of RFC 4301, that define which security algorithms and methods should be used when security associations are established. To help end users select the desired security levels for communications protected by IPsec, implementers may wish to provide a mechanism in the IKE policy databases to limit the mixing of security levels or to restrict combinations of protocols.

Security downgrade attacks, where more secure methods are deleted or modified from a payload by a man in the middle to force lower levels of security, are not a significant concern in IKEv2 Authentication payloads, because a modified AUTH payload will be detected when the peer computes a signature over the IKE messages. One specific class of downgrade attacks requires the selection of catastrophically weak ciphers, in which the attacker is able to break the cryptography in real time; this should be blocked by policy regarding cipher algorithm selection.

The hash algorithm registry does not include MD5, as it is not considered safe enough for signature use. The current IKEv2 protocol uses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, which has known security vulnerabilities and does not allow newer padding methods such as RSASSA-PSS; the new method described in the RFC allows the use of other padding methods. The current IKEv2 protocol also only allows normal DSA with SHA-1, which limits the security of the authentication to the security of SHA-1, and the new method allows using longer keys and longer hashes with DSA.
sections.plainLanguage:
The flexibility that the new method brings has a price. Because the curve and the hash are no longer tied together, an implementation could combine a strong curve with a weak hash, and the result would be as weak as its weakest part. The RFC therefore suggests that the policy databases of an IKE implementation should be able to restrict which combinations are allowed, so that an operator can set a floor on the security level.

Downgrade attacks are not a concern here, because the signature is computed over the whole exchange, so any change to a payload is detected when the signature is checked. The exception is the case where the attacker can break the cryptography outright, which has to be prevented by the cipher policy.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC creates a new IANA registry for IKEv2 hash algorithms, with changes and additions by Expert Review. The initial values of the registry are RESERVED with value 0, SHA1 with value 1, SHA2-256 with value 2, SHA2-384 with value 3 and SHA2-512 with value 4. MD5 is not included, as it is not considered safe enough for signature hash uses. Values 5 to 1023 are unassigned, and values 1024 to 65535 are reserved for private use among mutually consenting parties.

The specification also adds a new value for SIGNATURE_HASH_ALGORITHMS, 16431, to the IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Status Types registry, and a new value for Digital Signature, 14, to the IKEv2 Authentication Method registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The document starts two new registries. One lists the hash functions that may be used for signatures, with numbers for SHA-1 and the three SHA-2 sizes, and a block of numbers reserved for private use. The other records the new authentication method and the new notification type.
